### logline  <novel/outline/logline.md>

In the summer of 1956, in Windsor, a private, unpublicized encounter between the reigning Queen and a Hollywood starlet reconfigures their understandings of duty and celebrity; each must decide whether secrecy or revelation will shape their private lives and public faces.

### narrative-voice  <novel/style/voice.md>

Narration: third person omniscient, past tense. This was decided for the whole book before any of it was written and does not change.
Check your own sentences against it before you stage them. Mixing a collective "we" into a third-person narration, or slipping into present tense for a scene that feels immediate, is scored as a defect and is the most common one this system has produced: seven of nine consistency errors in a measured 18,000-word manuscript were exactly this.
If you think the story genuinely needs a different voice, propose the deviation — do not simply write it.

### world-rules  <world/rules.yaml>

These govern what is TRUE. They do not say what anyone KNOWS.
A character knows a rule only where canon says so; otherwise they may be ignorant of it, wrong about it, or in the middle of working it out — and if the story is about someone discovering one of these, writing it into their thoughts early is how that story gets destroyed.

- No anachronistic technology or cultural references: 1956 period-appropriate items only (no mobile phones, internet, social media, or modern slang).
- Do not invent major historical events or alter recorded history in consequential ways; the encounter is personal and private and must not trigger real-world geopolitical changes.
- Royal protocol and chain-of-command in 1950s Britain may be dramatized but should remain plausible; staff speak and act within plausible constraints of loyalty and discretion.
- Public reactions are constrained by 1950s press practices: newsreels, print newspapers, wire services and gossip columns, not instant global dissemination.
- Characters' ages and relationships to real historical figures must be plausible for 1956 and must not attribute historically impossible actions to real public figures beyond the contained fictional encounter.

The castle took the heat first, then gave it back in long waves. Sun climbed over the parapets and fell in bands across the river-facing windows; stone warmed until it smelled faintly of dust and bees. In the Queen’s private study the light leaned on heavy furniture and the curtains had been pulled so that the room kept something of the morning in reserve.

She sat at the desk as if she were keeping a polite vigil. Papers were arranged in a small, careful fan—dispatches, a single note in a hand she recognised, a photograph with one corner thumbed by a real thumb, not a glove. The air close to her was cooler than the rest of the room, the world held at the end of a sleeve. She did not rush. When she moved her hand it was to touch. Her finger traced the cool oval of the emerald brooch set on its velvet pad, feeling the rise of the setting and the tiny points of metal that held the stone—a gesture between inspection and reassurance.

The morning had the hush of ceremony without the formality. She had not yet dressed for the day; she wore instead a faded silk dressing gown whose small rose pattern looked younger than the stitching, slippers at her feet, and a thin chain at her throat on which a pendant caught the window light. The dispatches lay open; she made a brief pencil note at the bottom of one and folded it, as if to keep what she had put there safe enough for her to return to.

Prince Philip came and went like a punctuation. He crossed the tiled landing, cap in hand, offered a dry word that was equal parts account and apology—his shoulders carrying the boaty tiredness he had with him always—and took his leave for the morning’s errands. He walked the corridor with his hand lightly on a banister, feeling the day for its faults and its courtesies: the silver that needed a polish, the napkin fold that would not take the crease it should. She did not shout or make an announcement; instead she threaded through the cafés and the newsagent with the quiet authority of someone who knew headlines before they were written.

There was a small ceremony in these private acts, an agreement between the woman and the office she held. She took the file the press liaison had labelled Windsor and, with a brief look at the river as if it might keep a counsel for her, left the study.

Outside, the day spread itself like a promise or a challenge—one could not tell which yet. The castle breathed: the stables, the polished cars, the servants’ small adjustments and the town’s easy currents. The castle took the heat first, then gave it back in long waves. Sun climbed over the parapets and fell in bands across the river-facing windows; stone warmed until it smelled faintly of dust and bees. In the Queen’s private study the light leaned on heavy furniture and the curtains had been pulled so that the room kept something of the morning in reserve.

She sat at the desk as if she were keeping a polite vigil. Papers were arranged in a small, careful fan—dispatches, a single note in a hand she recognised, a photograph with one corner thumbed by a real thumb, not a glove. The air close to her was cooler than the rest of the room, the world held at the end of a sleeve. She did not rush. When she moved her hand it was to touch. Her finger traced the cool oval of the emerald brooch set on its velvet pad, feeling the rise of the setting and the tiny points of metal that held the stone—a gesture between inspection and reassurance.

The morning had the hush of ceremony without the formality. She had not yet dressed for the day; she wore instead a faded silk dressing gown whose small rose pattern looked younger than the stitching, slippers at her feet, and a thin chain at her throat on which a pendant caught the window light. The dispatches lay open; she made a brief pencil note at the bottom of one and folded it, as if to keep what she had put there safe enough for her to return to.

Prince Philip came and went like a punctuation. He crossed the tiled landing, cap in hand, offered a dry word that was equal parts account and apology—his shoulders carrying the boaty tiredness he had with him always—and took his leave for the morning’s errands. The moment he left the room it rearranged itself; the small tension in the air relaxed and the Queen resumed her nearer work, the ritual of state and of private continuity braided into each other in the quiet.

Outside the private apartments the house was all small motions. In the servant’s wing the royal butler moved with a long-schooled economy, a man who saw the house in parts and could tell from a footfall whether the day would be easy. He walked the corridor with his hand lightly on a banister, feeling the day for its faults and its courtesies: the silver that needed a polish, the napkin fold that would not take the crease it should. He was a guardian of angles and silence.

At the same time the lady-in-waiting prepared what the day required. In a small, bright room that smelled of starch and lemon she laid out gloves white as bone, a starched blouse, and a blue day dress folded so that its shoulders held no creases. She moved with the economy of one whose work was intimacy and management both; she smoothed the gown with the back of a hand as if flattening a tide. There was an attentiveness in her movements that read as both professional devotion and private deferral: each item chosen to make the sovereign legible in public.

From the stables came the ordinary counterpoint to palace stillness: the smell of hay and warm horse, the low thud of iron on wood as harnesses were checked, a boy’s whistle from somewhere where the sun did not yet reach. The stables carried the day’s pragmatism—feed, tack, water—the sound of things being placed in order so that the rest of the place could be otherwise. It was the household’s undercurrent, where loyalties were spoken in small grins and in the way a groom made a sure knot.

In the yard a pair of limousines waited, dark and patient. The royal chauffeur, cap brim perfectly rounded, ran a cloth across the chrome until his palm left no streak. He folded his gloved hand over the steering wheel and watched the morning like a man waiting for permission. The cars were not yet in motion; they were machines of readiness—clean leather, a faint smell of polish and petrol—that marked the difference between private passage and procession. He would choose the routes in which the town’s eye did not rest on them.

The press liaison sat for a time in the antechamber with a small pile of cuttings and the photograph the Queen had set aside. His fingers worried at the edge of a column; his face contained both calculation and a habit of being ready to soothe. Newspapers had a weight to their pages that was not simply print: they considered and conserved the day. He folded one clipping, making a deliberate crease, and slid it into a file labelled, without flourish, Windsor.

Word had travelled through Windsor by breakfast and by the polite signal of a telephone call: a famous actress was in the town, staying at the Castle View hotel. The actress’s publicist, a small, sharp woman who had the practised air of someone who organised not only schedules but reputations, stood on the high street for a moment and adjusted the strap of her handbag as if she were tightening an idea into place. She did not shout or make an announcement; instead she threaded through the cafés and the newsagent with the quiet authority of someone who knew headlines before they were written.

None of this was noise against the day so much as its texture. On the river quay the Thames lay warm, its surface folded in lazy ripples. Willows leaned as if to listen; a small motor launch drifted beyond the moorings and a group of tourists shaded their eyes and watched the castle in a summer hush. Heat lay on the stone of the bridge, and the high street hummed with a softened business: a grocer sweeping his door, a boy selling cold bottles of lemonade, the distant rat-tat of a varnisher’s brush.

The Queen rose when the hour came, folded the gown about her with a sovereign’s small habitual care, and set the emerald brooch back into its case with the same slow deliberation she had applied to the dispatches. There was a small ceremony in these private acts, an agreement between the woman and the office she held. She took the file the press liaison had labelled Windsor and, with a brief look at the river as if it might keep a counsel for her, left the study.

Outside, the day spread itself like a promise or a challenge—one could not tell which yet. The castle breathed: the stables, the polished cars, the servants’ small adjustments and the town’s easy currents. Under the warm, steady sun the river went on and the willows kept leaning, as if to whisper that the morning had time enough. The house, patient and composed, readied itself for whatever visitors might arrive beneath that light.

The limousine eased up under a shallow canopy of the Hotel Castle View and then stopped, long black like a beetle drawn close to the hotel's pale brick. The chauffeur opened the rear door with a motion practiced enough to look casual. Porters came forward in a small choreography—gloves, trunks, a hand to a shoulder—while the summer light folded itself across polished badges and brass handrails. The smell of petrol and a too-bright perfume threaded the warm air; someone had forgotten a hat on the pavement and it lay like an unclaimed promise.

She stepped out as if she had been practising it all her life: hat low enough to shade the face, gloves pale against her day dress, sunglasses lifted from her hair for the brief courtesy of the doorway. The movement turned the hotel into its stage. A camera-reflex would have loved her, but there were only a few late-morning strollers and a boy sweeping leaves; the presence around her was not a crowd but a sheen—an expectation that some spectacle might arrive if one only waited long enough.

Her driver, a steady man with white hair at the temples, took the suitcases with the half-manner of someone who had once been a valet. He did not loiter. The publicist touched the actress’s wrist once—a small, efficient adjustment of cuff and astringency—and then stepped back to the newsagent’s window where she bought today’s paper with the same quick attention she gave a contract. She did not read it in public. Instead she slid it to the newsagent with a folded finger, offered a tight smile, and whispered something that made the man tuck the paper into his counter drawer rather than display it on the rack. A small, private arrangement: where the paper might speak loudly, she had the power to ask it to be quiet.

The hotel’s ground floor breathed of bottled shampoo, a polish for furniture and the faint iron of boiled eggs on the chef’s silver trolley. A porter escorted them under the tawny sweep of the stairs to the lift; the lift rose with an obedient hum. The suite opened into a room that seemed to be built to take the act of being seen apart from the act of being alone. Lacquered furniture caught the light in thin, glossy stripes; a mirrored dressing table stood beneath a row of concealed bulbs that would, later tonight, make faces look as if lit from within. Script pages lay at an angle on a small writing desk, their corners weighted by a make-up case and a silver cigarette case that had been carried too often to be new.

She set her valise down and let her fingers travel, once, over the cigarette case as if expecting the same steadiness from the metal. It was cool and marked with a hairline scratch near the clasp. She opened it not to smoke but to order the small private ritual of checking what belonged to her. Inside, a lined card had been slipped between the cigarettes—an arrival note from the publicist and a pressing list, neat as a ledger. She did not read it aloud. The gesture was private; the objects kept their authority by staying quiet.

The publicist had what looked like a folder of clippings tucked under her elbow, a small, sensible stack that smelled faintly of citrus from a handkerchief. She spoke in low, pointed phrases: no interviews for the morning, meet the mayor after tea, no photographs on the balcony. The actress listened; the listening was a posture she knew better than the words. The confidante stood by the window, elbows on the sill, and offered an observation that availed itself of both wit and weariness. “You look at that roofline and tell me which of us has the better costume,” she said, voice dry. “They’ve saved the fancy for the stonework.”

The actress laughed, a short sound, and went to the window. Windsor folded itself in miniature beneath her—a scatter of slate roofs, a distant parapet, the river like a ribbon of pewter threading through the town. The castle’s roofline broke the horizon; she found herself looking at it with the same attention she gave a crew-chief’s instruction. It made a private map in her head: where a hat might catch a breeze, where a line of stone might throw a shadow across a camera. For a moment the landscape and the publicity were the same thing—a surface to negotiate and to be made to look inevitable.

Down on the high street the publicist’s small arrangement at the newsagent had been another action in a longer choreography. She had the habit of carrying clippings—what she called the ledger of sentiment—folded like a note, and she showed them to the actress as if they were talismans to be consulted. “See that?” she said, tapping a paragraph with a neat thumbnail. “They’ll paint you as the season’s ornament if we let them. Keep the balcony until after tea and we tell the right paper first.”

The confidante watched the actress with an economy that had the shape of long acquaintance. She was the kind of friend who had learned to count the time of a public face: how long it could hold a smile before fatigue cracked it, how many autographs were practical before an elbowed hand became a story. “If anyone asks,” she said, “we came for the river and stayed for the scenery.” She meant both. The actress, without looking back, slid the cigarette case closed and set it beside the make-up brushes as if the act completed something in the room.

A bell tinkled in the corridor as a footman announced—politely but with an authority concealed in the syllables—that lunch service would begin in the garden-dining room at half past. The publicist checked her watch, then folded the clippings and slid them into an inner pocket. The sheen of publicity, which had been only suggestion and appetite when the car had drawn up, settled into a plan: times, places, what would be shown and what would be kept out of sight. It was a map everyone understood now, even if they would not say it.

She turned back once more to the window. The river caught the light like a strip of quicksilver, and someone far below laughed—an ordinary sound, not for the cameras. For all its practiced glamour, she felt unexpectedly small, as if the glass between the hotel and the palace could not protect her from being seen in ways she had not practised. She lifted the sunglasses back into place and tilted her face to meet the room’s bulbs, the small light that would make her spectacles useless and her face legible instead.

The day was not yet a scene; it was a list of possibilities. She folded her hands on the dressing table and, when the footman’s polite knock came again—this time with a card—she put a finger to the small name-plate and read the single word it bore. It was not a public announcement. It was, simply, a beginning.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

The limousine eased up under a shallow canopy of the Hotel Castle View and then stopped, long black like a beetle drawn close to the hotel's pale brick. The chauffeur opened the rear door with a motion practiced enough to look casual. Porters came forward in a small choreography—gloves, trunks, a hand to a shoulder—while the summer light folded itself across polished badges and brass handrails. The smell of petrol and a too-bright perfume threaded the warm air; someone had forgotten a hat on the pavement and it lay like an unclaimed promise.

She stepped out as if she had been practising it all her life: hat low enough to shade the face, gloves pale against her day dress, sunglasses lifted from her hair for the brief courtesy of the doorway. The movement turned the hotel into its stage. A camera-reflex would have loved her, but there were only a few late-morning strollers and a boy sweeping leaves; the presence around her was not a crowd but a sheen—an expectation that some spectacle might arrive if one only waited long enough.

Her driver, a steady man with white hair at the temples, took the suitcases with the half-manner of someone who had once been a valet. He did not loiter. The publicist touched the actress’s wrist once—a small, efficient adjustment of cuff and astringency—and then stepped back to the newsagent’s window where she bought today’s paper with the same quick attention she gave a contract. She did not read it in public. Instead she slid it to the newsagent with a folded finger, offered a tight smile, and whispered something that made the man tuck the paper into his counter drawer rather than display it on the rack. A small, private arrangement: where the paper might speak loudly, she had the power to ask it to be quiet.

The hotel’s ground floor breathed of bottled shampoo, a polish for furniture and the faint iron of boiled eggs on the chef’s silver trolley. A porter escorted them under the tawny sweep of the stairs to the lift; the lift rose with an obedient hum. The suite opened into a room that seemed to be built to take the act of being seen apart from the act of being alone. Lacquered furniture caught the light in thin, glossy stripes; a mirrored dressing table stood beneath a row of concealed bulbs that would, later tonight, make faces look as if lit from within. Script pages lay at an angle on a small writing desk, their corners weighted by a make-up case and a silver cigarette case that had been carried too often to be new.

She set her valise down and let her fingers travel, once, over the cigarette case as if expecting the same steadiness from the metal. It was cool and marked with a hairline scratch near the clasp. She opened it not to smoke but to order the small private ritual of checking what belonged to her. Inside, a lined card had been slipped between the cigarettes—an arrival note from the publicist and a pressing list, neat as a ledger. She did not read it aloud. The gesture was private; the objects kept their authority by staying quiet.

The publicist had what looked like a folder of clippings tucked under her elbow, a small, sensible stack that smelled faintly of citrus from a handkerchief. She spoke in low, pointed phrases: no interviews for the morning, meet the mayor after tea, no photographs on the balcony. The actress listened; the listening was a posture she knew better than the words. The confidante stood by the window, elbows on the sill, and offered an observation that availed itself of both wit and weariness. “You look at that roofline and tell me which of us has the better costume,” she said, voice dry. “They’ve saved the fancy for the stonework.”

The actress laughed, a short sound, and went to the window. Windsor folded itself in miniature beneath her—a scatter of slate roofs, a distant parapet, the river like a ribbon of pewter threading through the town. The castle’s roofline broke the horizon; she found herself looking at it with the same attention she gave a crew-chief’s instruction. It made a private map in her head: where a hat might catch a breeze, where a line of stone might throw a shadow across a camera. For a moment the landscape and the publicity were the same thing—a surface to negotiate and to be made to look inevitable.

Down on the high street the publicist’s small arrangement at the newsagent had been another action in a longer choreography. She had the habit of carrying clippings—what she called the ledger of sentiment—folded like a note, and she showed them to the actress as if they were talismans to be consulted. “See that?” she said, tapping a paragraph with a neat thumbnail. “They’ll paint you as the season’s ornament if we let them. Keep the balcony until after tea and we tell the right paper first.”

The confidante watched the actress with an economy that had the shape of long acquaintance. She was the kind of friend who had learned to count the time of a public face: how long it could hold a smile before fatigue cracked it, how many autographs were practical before an elbowed hand became a story. “If anyone asks,” she said, “we came for the river and stayed for the scenery.” She meant both. The actress, without looking back, slid the cigarette case closed and set it beside the make-up brushes as if the act completed something in the room.

A bell tinkled in the corridor as a footman announced—politely but with an authority concealed in the syllables—that lunch service would begin in the garden-dining room at half past. The publicist checked her watch, then folded the clippings and slid them into an inner pocket. The sheen of publicity, which had been only suggestion and appetite when the car had drawn up, settled into a plan: times, places, what would be shown and what would be kept out of sight. It was a map everyone understood now, even if they would not say it.

She turned back once more to the window. The river caught the light like a strip of quicksilver, and someone far below laughed—an ordinary sound, not for the cameras. For all its practiced glamour, she felt unexpectedly small, as if the glass between the hotel and the palace could not protect her from being seen in ways she had not practised. She lifted the sunglasses back into place and tilted her face to meet the room’s bulbs, the small light that would make her spectacles useless and her face legible instead.

The day was not yet a scene; it was a list of possibilities. She folded her hands on the dressing table and, when the footman’s polite knock came again—this time with a card—she put a finger to the small name-plate and read the single word it bore. It was not a public announcement. It was, simply, a beginning.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-002.md>

The limousine eased up under a shallow canopy of the Hotel Castle View and then stopped, long black like a beetle drawn close to the hotel's pale brick. The chauffeur opened the rear door with a motion practiced enough to look casual. Porters came forward in a small choreography—gloves, trunks, a hand to a shoulder—while the summer light folded itself across polished badges and brass handrails. The smell of petrol and a too-bright perfume threaded the warm air; someone had forgotten a hat on the pavement and it lay like an unclaimed promise.

She stepped out as if she had been practising it all her life: hat low enough to shade the face, gloves pale against her day dress, sunglasses lifted from her hair for the brief courtesy of the doorway. The movement turned the hotel into its stage. A camera-reflex would have loved her, but there were only a few late-morning strollers and a boy sweeping leaves; the presence around her was not a crowd but a sheen—an expectation that some spectacle might arrive if one only waited long enough.

Her driver, a steady man with white hair at the temples, took the suitcases with the half-manner of someone who had once been a valet. He did not loiter. The publicist touched the actress’s wrist once—a small, efficient adjustment of cuff and astringency—and then stepped back to the newsagent’s window where she bought today’s paper with the same quick attention she gave a contract. She did not read it in public. Instead she slid it to the newsagent with a folded finger, offered a tight smile, and whispered something that made the man tuck the paper into his counter drawer rather than display it on the rack. A small, private arrangement: where the paper might speak loudly, she had the power to ask it to be quiet.

The hotel’s ground floor breathed of bottled shampoo, a polish for furniture and the faint iron of boiled eggs on the chef’s silver trolley. A porter escorted them under the tawny sweep of the stairs to the lift; the lift rose with an obedient hum. The suite opened into a room that seemed to be built to take the act of being seen apart from the act of being alone. Lacquered furniture caught the light in thin, glossy stripes; a mirrored dressing table stood beneath a row of concealed bulbs that would, later tonight, make faces look as if lit from within. Script pages lay at an angle on a small writing desk, their corners weighted by a make-up case and a silver cigarette case that had been carried too often to be new.

She set her valise down and let her fingers travel, once, over the cigarette case as if expecting the same steadiness from the metal. It was cool and marked with a hairline scratch near the clasp. She opened it not to smoke but to order the small private ritual of checking what belonged to her. Inside, a lined card had been slipped between the cigarettes—an arrival note from the publicist and a pressing list, neat as a ledger. She did not read it aloud. The gesture was private; the objects kept their authority by staying quiet.

The publicist had what looked like a folder of clippings tucked under her elbow, a small, sensible stack that smelled faintly of citrus from a handkerchief. She spoke in low, pointed phrases: no interviews for the morning, meet the mayor after tea, no photographs on the balcony. The actress listened; the listening was a posture she knew better than the words. The confidante stood by the window, elbows on the sill, and offered an observation that availed itself of both wit and weariness. “You look at that roofline and tell me which of us has the better costume,” she said, voice dry. “They’ve saved the fancy for the stonework.”

The actress laughed, a short sound, and went to the window. Windsor folded itself in miniature beneath her—a scatter of slate roofs, a distant parapet, the river like a ribbon of pewter threading through the town. The castle’s roofline broke the horizon; she found herself looking at it with the same attention she gave a crew-chief’s instruction. It made a private map in her head: where a hat might catch a breeze, where a line of stone might throw a shadow across a camera. For a moment the landscape and the publicity were the same thing—a surface to negotiate and to be made to look inevitable.

Down on the high street the publicist’s small arrangement at the newsagent had been another action in a longer choreography. She had the habit of carrying clippings—what she called the ledger of sentiment—folded like a note, and she showed them to the actress as if they were talismans to be consulted. “See that?” she said, tapping a paragraph with a neat thumbnail. “They’ll paint you as the season’s ornament if we let them. Keep the balcony until after tea and we tell the right paper first.”

The confidante watched the actress with an economy that had the shape of long acquaintance. She was the kind of friend who had learned to count the time of a public face: how long it could hold a smile before fatigue cracked it, how many autographs were practical before an elbowed hand became a story. “If anyone asks,” she said, “we came for the river and stayed for the scenery.” She meant both. The actress, without looking back, slid the cigarette case closed and set it beside the make-up brushes as if the act completed something in the room.

A bell tinkled in the corridor as a footman announced—politely but with an authority concealed in the syllables—that lunch service would begin in the garden-dining room at half past. The publicist checked her watch, then folded the clippings and slid them into an inner pocket. The sheen of publicity, which had been only suggestion and appetite when the car had drawn up, settled into a plan: times, places, what would be shown and what would be kept out of sight. It was a map everyone understood now, even if they would not say it.

She turned back once more to the window. The river caught the light like a strip of quicksilver, and someone far below laughed—an ordinary sound, not for the cameras. For all its practiced glamour, she felt unexpectedly small, as if the glass between the hotel and the palace could not protect her from being seen in ways she had not practised. She lifted the sunglasses back into place and tilted her face to meet the room’s bulbs, the small light that would make her spectacles useless and her face legible instead.

The day was not yet a scene; it was a list of possibilities. She folded her hands on the dressing table and, when the footman’s polite knock came again—this time with a card—she put a finger to the small name-plate and read the single word it bore. It was not a public announcement. It was, simply, a beginning.

The high street of Windsor lay in a late-summer softness, heat going out of the stones as if the town were taking a deep, polite breath. Early shutters were open: a grocer’s awning striped white and green, a tear in a poster at the noticeboard for a repertory season, the tea-room’s windows steamed with fresh pots. A milkman in a white smock shouldered a crate, a varnisher knelt over a banister with a tin of gloss, and a boy pushed a tray of lemonade between the tourists’ legs like a steady, sunburned metronome. Hats and collars and the small commerce of mornings gave the street its rhythm.

Tom Harris had the best place to see it. He stood on the step of Harris & Sons, towel at his waist, one hand on the brass rail he’d polished that morning. He was a man who had learned to read the town in half a dozen gestures: the scuff of a brogue that suggested whether a man paid his rent on Friday or fancied himself a gentleman, the ink-stained thumb of the printer’s apprentice, the way a vicar removed his hat in the shop and set it on the counter like an offering. Tom had kept rooms above the shop for fifty years and could place a new arrival by the knock.

“Good morning,” he said to no one and everyone, sweeping the last grit off the door-mat. His voice was the mild, slightly ironic voice of someone who had watched generations of summer suits come and go. He nodded at the noticeboard where a poster for the theatre had curled; he flicked his finger at the newsagent’s window where a neat pile of cuttings had been set behind glass. “Langley’s keeps a tidy file,” he observed, as if that explained the world.

Langley’s Newsagents did keep a tidy file. Inside, a publicist—small, efficient, orange silk handkerchief to the cheek—moved like a woman with a plan. She glanced out, checked the clippings she carried, and made a faint sign to the newsman that a copy was to be tucked away. The press cuttings showed in the window as a margin of headlines, but the publicist’s hand, the line of her mouth, meant the story could be managed. A stranger walking past might have thought the cuttings were for sale; the town read them as a ledger, a thing that might be consulted and argued with in the same breath.

The actress’s driver steered his car down past the Crown Tea Rooms with the calm of someone who had learned to make grand entrances feel incidental. His uniform was neat, his hands steady on the wheel, and he carried a case of luggage like a man who had done this for years. Almost at the same moment the royal chauffeur came the other way, cap pulled low, limousines idling behind him in the castle yard like patient beasts. The two men passed in the street—two professional courtesies, a half-nod, a measuring look—and the town adjusted its attention accordingly.

Where the drivers crossed, talk shifted from what a dress cost to what it meant that a royal car had used the lane. “They don’t come down here,” Tom said to a woman buying a lemon tart from the tea-room window. “Not regular-like. When they do, folks twitch.” He tilted his chin toward the castle roofline in the same way a man might point to weather: a fact that pleased and worried folk in equal measure.

Tourists clustered at the quay end of the street, cameras slung like talismans over their shoulders, while a few Windsor regulars—men in dark suits with trilby hats, shopgirls with neat aprons, children with short trousers and knotted handkerchiefs at their collars—went about the business of living. Women kept the thin gloves of daywear in their purses; hats tilted at an angle were as much a protection from the sun as a code. A clerk with ink at his cuff and a paper ration ticket folded in his breast watched the movement like anyone else who kept an eye on possible work. Differences existed and showed themselves in small things: the brogues that were scuffed at the toes carried a different story from the shoes shined until they barked back the sun.

The publicist moved out, a bright slash among the shopfronts, and the newsman slipped a newspaper behind the counter with a practiced hand. The file of press cuttings—the same sort the palace man kept in a folder labelled Windsor—had become visible to anyone who cared to look. Tom harrumphed softly, more to fill the silence than from surprise. He had seen stars before, actresses who believed every passerby was their audience and gentlemen who disliked being noticed at all. The town made distinctions that were not unkind: celebrity could be enjoyed from a distance, whereas the royal household was something to be particularly careful about. “We clap for the pictures, sir,” he told the boy sweeping leaves, “but we take off our hats for the house.”

A motor launch slipped along the river where the parapet opened the view; a woman leaned against the rail, hat in hand, smiling at nothing a camera could catch. Above, in the hotel that looked down at the slate roofs, someone drew the blinds for privacy and let the ordinary light go on with its business. The street kept its small economy of gossip—what car had the new badges, who brought trunks to which hotel, whether a porter had been seen with a hat too fine for his station—and folded that economy into the larger fact of the castle’s presence.

When the actress’s driver stopped for a moment to let a bellboy wheel a case across the pavement, Tom tipped his hat with the old courtesy, not foolish but observational. He watched the glove as if it were the last word of a sentence. “Looks the part, don’t she,” he said in a tone that was not envy but appraisal; the woman at the tea-room smiled and nodded, then turned back to her pots. 

The day had the pleasant, particular air of a town that expected to be admired and to ignore the admiration in measured turns. Windsor, Tom knew, had always been a place of carefully held attention: you noticed what mattered, you kept your ledger of whom you watched and why, and you kept most of your talk for the evening when the lids came down and the shutters closed. For now the high street kept to its rhythm—hovers of tourists, the precise commerce of shopkeepers, two chauffeurs passing on business the town would speak of over lemon tarts—and the noticeboard, with its curling poster, looked on like a patient neighbour.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

The high street of Windsor lay in a late-summer softness, heat going out of the stones as if the town were taking a deep, polite breath. Early shutters were open: a grocer’s awning striped white and green, a tear in a poster at the noticeboard for a repertory season, the tea-room’s windows steamed with fresh pots. A milkman in a white smock shouldered a crate, a varnisher knelt over a banister with a tin of gloss, and a boy pushed a tray of lemonade between the tourists’ legs like a steady, sunburned metronome. Hats and collars and the small commerce of mornings gave the street its rhythm.

Tom Harris had the best place to see it. He stood on the step of Harris & Sons, towel at his waist, one hand on the brass rail he’d polished that morning. He was a man who had learned to read the town in half a dozen gestures: the scuff of a brogue that suggested whether a man paid his rent on Friday or fancied himself a gentleman, the ink-stained thumb of the printer’s apprentice, the way a vicar removed his hat in the shop and set it on the counter like an offering. Tom had kept rooms above the shop for fifty years and could place a new arrival by the knock.

“Good morning,” he said to no one and everyone, sweeping the last grit off the door-mat. His voice was the mild, slightly ironic voice of someone who had watched generations of summer suits come and go. He nodded at the noticeboard where a poster for the theatre had curled; he flicked his finger at the newsagent’s window where a neat pile of cuttings had been set behind glass. The file of press cuttings—already familiar to the palace man—showed in the window now, and Tom noted the neat pile as proof the town read reputation like a ledger.

Inside Langley’s Newsagents a publicist—small, efficient, orange silk handkerchief to the cheek—moved with the precise economy of someone used to making stories behave. She stood long enough to make a small sign; the newsman slid a paper behind the counter without a show of it. That was no secret here: the pile in the window did the talking for them. Tom watched the exchange like a man who had learned that reputation was traded in margins and margins were read aloud.

The actress’s driver steered his car down past the Crown Tea Rooms with the calm of someone who had learned to make grand entrances feel incidental. His uniform was neat, his hands steady on the wheel, and he carried a case of luggage like a man who had done this for years. Almost at the same moment the royal chauffeur came the other way, cap pulled low, limousines idling behind him in the castle yard like patient beasts. The two men passed in the street—two professional courtesies, a half-nod, a measuring look—and Tom paused with his broom, blade of it resting on the step, to watch them go.

Tourists clustered at the quay end of the street, cameras slung like talismans over their shoulders. A woman with a straw hat angled against the sun laughed at something a companion said; a child thrust a hand into the pocket of a coat that was too big and kept hold of a cotton reel of candy. Windsor regulars moved through the scene: men in dark suits with trilby hats, shopgirls with neat aprons, children with short trousers and handkerchiefs knotted at their collars. Tom found small confirmations of his reading in the pause and the ways people set their hats or tucked a glove into a purse. A clerk with ink at his cuff watched from the doorway of the solicitor’s office, a theatre programme folded in his breast-pocket like something worth saving.

The publicist moved out, a bright slash among the shopfronts, and the newsman slipped a paper behind the counter with a practiced hand. The whole business of the cuttings—the same sort the palace man kept in a folder labelled Windsor—had become visible to anyone who cared to look. Tom harrumphed softly, more to fill the silence than from surprise. He had seen stars before, actresses who believed every passerby was their audience and gentlemen who disliked being noticed at all. The town made distinctions that were not unkind: celebrity could be enjoyed from a distance, whereas the royal household was something to be particularly careful about. “We clap for the pictures, sir,” he told the boy sweeping leaves, “but we take off our hats for the house.”

When the actress’s driver stopped for a moment to let a bellboy wheel a case across the pavement, Tom tipped his hat with the old courtesy, not foolish but observational. He watched the glove as if it were the last word of a sentence. “Looks the part, don’t she,” he said in a tone that was not envy but appraisal; the woman at the tea-room smiled and nodded, then turned back to her pots.

The day had the pleasant, particular air of a town that expected to be admired and to ignore the admiration in measured turns. Windsor, Tom knew, had always been a place of carefully held attention: you noticed what mattered, you kept your ledger of whom you watched and why, and you kept most of your talk for the evening when the lids came down and the shutters closed. For now the high street kept to its rhythm—hovers of tourists, the precise commerce of shopkeepers, two chauffeurs passing on business the town would speak of over lemon tarts—and the noticeboard, with its curling poster, looked on like a patient neighbour.

### previous-scene  <novel/chapters/ch-01/scenes/s-003.md>

The high street of Windsor lay in a late-summer softness, heat going out of the stones as if the town were taking a deep, polite breath. Early shutters were open: a grocer’s awning striped white and green, a tear in a poster at the noticeboard for a repertory season, the tea-room’s windows steamed with fresh pots. A milkman in a white smock shouldered a crate, a varnisher knelt over a banister with a tin of gloss, and a boy pushed a tray of lemonade between the tourists’ legs like a steady, sunburned metronome. Hats and collars and the small commerce of mornings gave the street its rhythm.

Tom Harris had the best place to see it. He stood on the step of Harris & Sons, towel at his waist, one hand on the brass rail he’d polished that morning. He was a man who had learned to read the town in half a dozen gestures: the scuff of a brogue that suggested whether a man paid his rent on Friday or fancied himself a gentleman, the ink-stained thumb of the printer’s apprentice, the way a vicar removed his hat in the shop and set it on the counter like an offering. Tom had kept rooms above the shop for fifty years and could place a new arrival by the knock.

“Good morning,” he said to no one and everyone, sweeping the last grit off the door-mat. His voice was the mild, slightly ironic voice of someone who had watched generations of summer suits come and go. He nodded at the noticeboard where a poster for the theatre had curled; he flicked his finger at the newsagent’s window where a neat pile of cuttings had been set behind glass. The file of press cuttings—already familiar to the palace man—showed in the window now, and Tom noted the neat pile as proof the town read reputation like a ledger.

Inside Langley’s Newsagents a publicist—small, efficient, orange silk handkerchief to the cheek—moved with the precise economy of someone used to making stories behave. She stood long enough to make a small sign; the newsman slid a paper behind the counter without a show of it. That was no secret here: the pile in the window did the talking for them. Tom watched the exchange like a man who had learned that reputation was traded in margins and margins were read aloud.

The actress’s driver steered his car down past the Crown Tea Rooms with the calm of someone who had learned to make grand entrances feel incidental. His uniform was neat, his hands steady on the wheel, and he carried a case of luggage like a man who had done this for years. Almost at the same moment the royal chauffeur came the other way, cap pulled low, limousines idling behind him in the castle yard like patient beasts. The two men passed in the street—two professional courtesies, a half-nod, a measuring look—and Tom paused with his broom, blade of it resting on the step, to watch them go.

Tourists clustered at the quay end of the street, cameras slung like talismans over their shoulders. A woman with a straw hat angled against the sun laughed at something a companion said; a child thrust a hand into the pocket of a coat that was too big and kept hold of a cotton reel of candy. Windsor regulars moved through the scene: men in dark suits with trilby hats, shopgirls with neat aprons, children with short trousers and handkerchiefs knotted at their collars. Tom found small confirmations of his reading in the pause and the ways people set their hats or tucked a glove into a purse. A clerk with ink at his cuff watched from the doorway of the solicitor’s office, a theatre programme folded in his breast-pocket like something worth saving.

The publicist moved out, a bright slash among the shopfronts, and the newsman slipped a paper behind the counter with a practiced hand. The whole business of the cuttings—the same sort the palace man kept in a folder labelled Windsor—had become visible to anyone who cared to look. Tom harrumphed softly, more to fill the silence than from surprise. He had seen stars before, actresses who believed every passerby was their audience and gentlemen who disliked being noticed at all. The town made distinctions that were not unkind: celebrity could be enjoyed from a distance, whereas the royal household was something to be particularly careful about. “We clap for the pictures, sir,” he told the boy sweeping leaves, “but we take off our hats for the house.”

When the actress’s driver stopped for a moment to let a bellboy wheel a case across the pavement, Tom tipped his hat with the old courtesy, not foolish but observational. He watched the glove as if it were the last word of a sentence. “Looks the part, don’t she,” he said in a tone that was not envy but appraisal; the woman at the tea-room smiled and nodded, then turned back to her pots.

The day had the pleasant, particular air of a town that expected to be admired and to ignore the admiration in measured turns. Windsor, Tom knew, had always been a place of carefully held attention: you noticed what mattered, you kept your ledger of whom you watched and why, and you kept most of your talk for the evening when the lids came down and the shutters closed. For now the high street kept to its rhythm—hovers of tourists, the precise commerce of shopkeepers, two chauffeurs passing on business the town would speak of over lemon tarts—and the noticeboard, with its curling poster, looked on like a patient neighbour.

The royal butler showed the press liaison in with a hand that did not linger; his face was the house’s ledger—polite, economical, not in the habit of giving more than the day demanded.

The press liaison set the bundle on the desk and smoothed the top clipping with a forefinger as if straightening a thought. He worked in the neat language of small decisions: make an introduction, refuse a photograph, time a paragraph. The newspapers smelled faintly of ink and lemon peel; under the string the file was labelled Windsor, the handwriting familiar enough to be a signature of the household’s attention.

"It came in before breakfast," the butler said. "Miss Langley passed this on."

He left them with the door half-ajar. The press liaison made a sound that was nearly a laugh and untied the string. He spread the clippings like a patient physician, pointing at a gossip column, a photograph with a thumbed corner, a wire story that had picked up a remark from a provincial correspondent. He kept a photograph to one side and let the paper rustle; the sound suited the day.

When the lady-in-waiting arrived she closed the door with the exacting politeness of someone who kept her house in order. Her voice in the little room had the same careful cadence it had at the Queen’s shoulder: measured, private, and immediately protective.

"Good morning," she said. She did not sit. "You will have seen about our visitor."

He nodded and laid a clipping in front of her. "Miss Cavendish is staying at the Castle View. Her publicist has been busy in town. I thought it best to bring you the file and to ask how we should proceed."

They worked with the same objects and different priorities. The press liaison’s fingers found the index card where he kept the names of newsreel men and the number of the provincial office in Reading. "There are a few options," he said. "We ask her publicist for a controlled photograph—staged, two or three frames—agree a short caption, and issue a brief wire. It gives the papers something that can’t be misread in a gossip column. The newsreels will take the frame if we hand it to them properly."

The lady-in-waiting touched the clipping as if it were something that might bruise. "And it places her in the path of cameras rather than away from them. The Queen’s mornings are for the Queen. We preserve that, if we can. Do you propose an introduction?"

"A formal introduction could be arranged," he said. "It would need the Queen’s agreement, and one of us would have to set the precise terms. If you prefer…we could keep any meeting private, notify no cameras, and let the press take their chances. My worry is the columns. Where there is a vacuum of fact, gossip fills it. If we must have the meeting—if the Queen wishes it—then it should be as private as possible, and only by her leave should it be made public."

He did not argue the principle; he argued the arithmetic. "The papers are already talking. The publicist has been through Langley’s; I’ve seen the pile myself. Allowing an uncontrolled scrum will give gossip columns more to invent than the facts would justify. I recommend we write a line—short, factual—supply a single photograph if necessary, and keep any further comment for Buckingham."

She considered the photograph the way one might consider an offered brooch—an item that could bind or betray. "Who signs off?" she asked.

The lady-in-waiting kept the private consequence in view. "If we set a photograph," she said, "we must set its bounds. No balcony shots, no evening promenades in costume—only the rooms she would be welcome in. If the Queen prefers not to receive her publicly, the household will make that case."

He wrote the options on a small memo and folded it to her. "I shall call Miss Cavendish’s publicist and put forward a controlled frame. I will also make an inquiry to Buckingham about whether any formal line should be issued from there. If the Queen wishes a private interview, we shall wait for her word."

"Then you will let me know before anything is given to the press," she said. "We do not speak for the sovereign without her leave."

"Of course." He stamped the memo with the soft pressure of a man who issued statements and lived to revise them. "I will also have the file of cuttings kept under lock until we decide."

She took the clipping, folded it once, and held it like a petition. "There is kindness in discretion," she said. "And harm in display."

He replaced the newspapers on the desk and tied them with the same brown string. "Then we shall keep the story honest and keep the morning honest as well. I will speak to the publicist in town first."
